title: Variational Learning with Sparse Long-range Entangling Gates
authors: Helene M. Lösl, Aydin Deger, Andrew J. Daley
abstract: The performance of variational quantum algorithms depends in general on the structure of the parametrized quantum circuit, but the most common ansätze are typically based on local couplings. Motivated by the extended connectivity available with neutral atoms and trapped ions, we examine when structured long-range connectivity provides a useful resource, focusing on sparse power-of-two (PWR2) coupling graphs. Using dynamical Lie-algebra analysis, approximate unitary-design diagnostics, and finite-depth measures of expressibility and entanglement, we examine how these geometries enlarge the accessible operator space. This enlarged space alone is not sufficient to ensure trainability of the parameterized circuit for given target problems, and we explore performance across example problems with and without long-range coupling, identifying where sparse coupling graphs are or are not likely to provide an advantage. We also introduce a variational scheme that maps hierarchical long-range Hamiltonians to geometrically local ones that can be optimized with short-range circuits. Together, these results identify circuit geometry and qubit reconfigurability as task-dependent resources for variational algorithms, relevant to ongoing developments in quantum hardware with long-range connectivity.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes how the physical connectivity of qubits impacts the performance of Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs). By comparing local versus structured long-range couplings (like PWR2), the authors show that specific geometries enhance the accessible operator space and improve VQE convergence. They conclude by proposing methods to effectively utilize these long-range interactions, making circuit geometry a key design parameter for quantum hardware.
main_problem: The study investigates whether structured long-range connectivity provides a computational advantage for Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) compared to standard local couplings.
main_result: Structured long-range coupling graphs, like the PWR2 graph, can offer an improved balance between circuit expressibility and depth for VQEs on systems like the TFIM. Furthermore, mapping hierarchical Hamiltonians to geometrically local ones via techniques like the Monna map is a viable optimization strategy.
method: The authors employ advanced diagnostics including dynamical Lie-algebra analysis, approximate unitary-design measurements ($\lambda_G$), finite-depth measures of expressibility (KL divergence), and variational schemes for Hamiltonian mapping.
model_or_system: The work models quantum systems using neutral atoms and trapped ions, which naturally support long-range entangling gates. The primary testbed is the Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM) solved via VQE, comparing Nearest Neighbor (NN), Power-of-Two (PWR2), and All-to-All (A2A) connectivity.
key_observables: Expressibility, entanglement capability (Meyer-Wallach entropy), commutator depth required to generate target algebras ($\mathfrak{so}(2n)$), and energy error $|\delta E|/\Delta$ in VQE simulations.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($L$), connectivity graph structure (NN vs. PWR2), transverse field strength ($B/J$), and the size of the system ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that circuit geometry and qubit reconfigurability are task-dependent resources for VQAs, though they caution that high expressibility does not guarantee trainability.
figures_summary: Figures compare coupling graphs (NN, PWR2, A2A), illustrate the Monna variational pipeline, show energy error vs. depth comparing NN and LR gates, and demonstrate mutual information localization after applying the Monna map.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical motivation for long-range connectivity in trapped ion platforms. It then uses rigorous mathematical tools (Lie algebra analysis) to compare the algebraic reach of different graph structures. Finally, it validates these theoretical findings through numerical VQE simulations and proposes practical mapping techniques.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations by providing a quantitative framework for selecting optimal qubit connectivity patterns for variational quantum algorithms, which is crucial for scaling up trapped-ion or neutral-atom quantum simulators.
